overview.old_value:
NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is a coenzyme found in every living cell, playing essential roles in energy metabolism, DNA repair, and gene expression regulation. It is a dinucleotide coenzyme, not a peptide.

NAD+ levels decline approximately 50% between ages 40 and 60, correlating with many hallmarks of aging including mitochondrial dysfunction, genomic instability, and cellular senescence. This age-related decline has positioned NAD+ supplementation as a central focus of longevity research.

Research interest spans neurodegenerative disease, aging biology, metabolic health, and addiction medicine.
overview.new_value:
NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is a coenzyme found in every living cell, playing essential roles in energy metabolism, DNA repair, and gene expression regulation. It is a dinucleotide coenzyme, not a peptide.

A decline in NAD+ has been linked to ageing and age-related disorders, mainly on the basis of animal studies. In people the evidence is limited. A 2025 review in Nature Metabolism found that an age-related fall in NAD+ has been consistently observed in only a limited number of human studies, and that data on NAD+ in human tissues remain sparse. Findings vary by tissue and by measurement method: a 2026 study of seven human cohorts, using a validated mass-spectrometry method, found that whole-blood NAD+ levels did not vary with age. Whether raising NAD+ benefits people is still an open research question.

Research interest spans neurodegenerative disease, aging biology, metabolic health, and addiction medicine.

background.old_value:
NAD+ was first discovered in 1906 by Arthur Harden during fermentation research. Its role in cellular energy production was elucidated over the following decades, earning multiple Nobel Prizes for researchers studying its biochemistry.

The modern era of NAD+ research began with the discovery that sirtuins — a family of enzymes linked to longevity — require NAD+ as a substrate. This connection, combined with the demonstration that NAD+ levels decline dramatically with age, catalyzed a surge of research into NAD+ supplementation.

Current research approaches include direct IV or subcutaneous NAD+ administration, as well as oral precursors like NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) and NR (nicotinamide riboside) that the body converts to NAD+.
background.new_value:
NAD+ was first described in 1906, when Arthur Harden and William John Young showed that a heat-stable factor in boiled yeast juice was needed for alcoholic fermentation (Proc R Soc Lond B 1906). The factor, later called cozymase, was characterised over the following decades; in 1936 Otto Warburg and Walter Christian identified its pyridine (nicotinamide) component as the part that transfers hydrogen (Helv Chim Acta 1936). Harden shared the 1929 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Hans von Euler-Chelpin "for their investigations on the fermentation of sugar and fermentative enzymes" (nobelprize.org).

The modern era of NAD+ research began with the discovery that sirtuins — a family of enzymes linked to longevity — require NAD+ as a substrate. This connection, combined with reports, mainly from rodent studies, that NAD+ levels decline with age, catalyzed a surge of research into NAD+ supplementation. Human evidence for an age-related decline is limited and varies by tissue and measurement method (see Overview).

Current research approaches include direct IV or subcutaneous NAD+ administration, as well as oral precursors like NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide) and NR (nicotinamide riboside) that the body converts to NAD+.

conclusion.old_value:
NAD+ occupies a unique position in cellular-energy and longevity research as the molecule that connects cellular energy production to the fundamental biology of aging. Its role as a substrate for sirtuins and PARPs places it at the intersection of metabolism, DNA repair, and gene regulation.

The age-related decline in NAD+ levels — approximately 50% between ages 40 and 60 — provides a clear biological rationale for supplementation research. Preclinical evidence for NAD+ restoration is among the most compelling in aging biology, with consistent demonstrations of improved healthspan across multiple model organisms.

Human evidence is growing but not yet definitive. IV NAD+ protocols have a track record in clinical settings, and oral precursor trials are generating encouraging data. The field awaits large-scale, long-term human trials to determine whether the dramatic preclinical benefits translate to meaningful human health improvements.

For researchers, NAD+ represents a well-characterized, mechanistically understood compound with extensive published literature and growing clinical evidence.
conclusion.new_value:
NAD+ occupies a unique position in cellular-energy and longevity research as the molecule that connects cellular energy production to the fundamental biology of aging. Its role as a substrate for sirtuins and PARPs places it at the intersection of metabolism, DNA repair, and gene regulation.

Whether NAD+ levels fall with age in people is less settled than often stated. Human data are limited and differ by tissue and measurement method, and a 2026 study of seven cohorts found that whole-blood NAD+ did not vary with age (Nat Metab 2025; Nat Metab 2026). Preclinical studies in several model organisms report benefits from raising NAD+, but rodent findings do not translate directly to people.

Human evidence is limited. A 2025 review found that clinical trials of NAD+ precursors have so far shown limited efficacy. The field awaits large-scale, long-term human trials to determine whether preclinical benefits translate to meaningful human health improvements.

For researchers, NAD+ represents a well-characterized, mechanistically understood compound with extensive published literature and a limited but growing body of clinical studies.

entries.value: NAD+ is not classified as a drug by the FDA. IV NAD+ is administered in clinical settings under physician supervision. Oral precursors NMN and NR are marketed as dietary supplements. In 2022, FDA issued a notice questioning NMN's status as a supplement due to its investigation as a drug candidate.

entries.value: NAD+ (nadide) is not the active ingredient of any FDA-approved drug. A search of Drugs@FDA (openFDA) on 19 Oct 2026 found no application listing it.

**Compounding lists:** FDA lists nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) in Category 1 (bulk drug substances under evaluation) of its list for compounding under section 503A (list updated 14 May 2026). It lists beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide in Category 1 of its list for outsourcing facilities under section 503B (list updated 21 Mar 2025). Under FDA's interim policies, FDA generally does not intend to take action against compounding with a Category 1 substance while the nomination is evaluated, if other conditions are met. This is enforcement discretion, not placement on a bulks list and not an approval. Beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide disodium salt trihydrate appears in Category 3 (nominated without adequate support) of both lists.

**Precursors:** nicotinamide riboside (NR) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) are NAD+ precursors, not NAD+ itself. Nicotinamide riboside chloride is also in Category 1 of FDA's 503B list. In letters of October and November 2022 to firms that had notified it of NMN as a new dietary ingredient, FDA said NMN was excluded from the definition of a dietary supplement because, in its view at the time, NMN had not been lawfully marketed as a supplement or food before it was authorized for investigation as a new drug. In a September 2025 response to a citizen petition (docket FDA-2023-P-0872), FDA reversed that position. It concluded that NMN is not excluded from the definition, because NMN was marketed as a dietary supplement in the United States before that authorization. In the same response FDA described NMN as a new dietary ingredient, so the new-dietary-ingredient notification requirements (section 413 of the FD&C Act) still apply. The response addressed only whether NMN is excluded from the supplement definition; it was not a safety finding.

entries.value: Intravenous NAD+ infusion has been used in clinical settings for over a decade, primarily in addiction medicine. BR+NAD (Brain Restoration Plus NAD) protocols, pioneered by clinics in the US and Australia, use slow IV infusion (500-1000mg over 4-8 hours) for substance withdrawal support.\n\nPatient-reported outcomes include reduced withdrawal symptoms, improved cognitive clarity, and decreased cravings. However, rigorous placebo-controlled trials specifically for IV NAD+ in addiction remain limited.

Multiple clinical trials have evaluated oral NMN and NR supplementation. A 2022 trial published in Science showed that NMN supplementation increased NAD+ levels and improved insulin sensitivity in prediabetic women. NR trials have demonstrated measurable NAD+ elevation in blood and improved metabolic markers in older adults.\n\nThe key question — whether raising NAD+ in humans produces the dramatic health benefits seen in mice — remains under active investigation.

new_value.title: Intravenous NAD+

entries.value: Intravenous NAD+ is offered in some clinical settings, including addiction medicine, but controlled human evidence is limited. A small human pilot study (Front Aging Neurosci 2019) found that, during an intravenous infusion, NAD+ was rapidly and completely removed from plasma for at least the first 2 hours, with a metabolite profile consistent with breakdown by NAD+-consuming enzymes; urinary products included NAD+ itself and methylnicotinamide. Two of its authors were affiliated with NAD+ Research Inc. and Springfield Wellness Center (Springfield, LA). The study was not designed to test clinical benefit.\n\nReports of reduced withdrawal symptoms, improved cognitive clarity or decreased cravings come from patient reports, not from rigorous placebo-controlled trials.

new_value.title: Oral Precursor Trials

entries.value: Multiple clinical trials have evaluated oral NMN and NR supplementation. In a 10-week randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese, NMN increased muscle insulin sensitivity (measured with a hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp), muscle insulin signaling and the expression of muscle-remodeling genes (Science 2021). Whole-blood NAD+ changes with NR supplementation (Nat Metab 2026). A 2025 review concluded that, overall, human trials of NAD+ precursors have shown limited efficacy (Nat Metab 2025).\n\nThe key question — whether raising NAD+ in humans produces the benefits reported in mice — remains under active investigation.

old_value.question: Is NAD+ a peptide?
old_value.answer: No. NAD+ is a dinucleotide coenzyme. It is a dinucleotide coenzyme, not a peptide.

old_value.question: Why are IV infusions so slow?
old_value.answer: Rapid NAD+ infusion causes uncomfortable side effects (nausea, chest pressure). Slow infusion over 2-6 hours is standard for tolerability.

old_value.question: How does NAD+ differ from NMN supplements?
old_value.answer: NMN is an oral precursor that the body converts into NAD+. IV NAD+ delivers the active coenzyme directly, bypassing conversion steps.

new_value.question: Is NAD+ a peptide?
new_value.answer: No. NAD+ is a dinucleotide coenzyme. It has no amino-acid sequence.

new_value.question: What is known about intravenous NAD+ in humans?
new_value.answer: Published human data are limited. A small human pilot study (Front Aging Neurosci 2019) found that, during an intravenous infusion, NAD+ was rapidly and completely removed from plasma for at least the first 2 hours, with a metabolite profile consistent with breakdown by NAD+-consuming enzymes; urinary products included NAD+ itself and methylnicotinamide. Two of its authors were affiliated with NAD+ Research Inc. and Springfield Wellness Center (Springfield, LA). The study was not designed to test clinical benefit.

new_value.question: How does NAD+ differ from NMN supplements?
new_value.answer: NMN is a precursor that cells convert into NAD+. In a small intravenous pilot, infused NAD+ was rapidly removed from plasma and its metabolites were consistent with breakdown by NAD+-cleaving enzymes, so it is not established that infused NAD+ reaches cells intact (Front Aging Neurosci 2019).

new_value.question: Do NAD+ levels fall with age in humans?
new_value.answer: The evidence is limited and inconsistent. A 2025 review found that an age-related decline has been consistently observed in only a limited number of human studies, and that data on human tissues remain sparse (Nat Metab 2025). Results vary by tissue and measurement method; a 2026 study of seven cohorts found that whole-blood NAD+ did not vary with age (Nat Metab 2026).

new_value.question: Is NAD+ an FDA-approved drug?
new_value.answer: No, as of 19 Oct 2026. FDA lists NAD in Category 1 of its 503A list and beta-nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide in Category 1 of its 503B list. That is enforcement discretion while nominations are evaluated, not placement on a bulks list and not an approval.

new_value.question: What is FDA's position on NMN as a dietary supplement?
new_value.answer: In 2022 FDA said NMN was excluded from the dietary-supplement definition. In a September 2025 response to a citizen petition (docket FDA-2023-P-0872), FDA reversed that position and concluded that NMN is not excluded, because it was marketed as a dietary supplement in the United States before it was authorized for investigation as a new drug. FDA described NMN as a new dietary ingredient, so notification rules still apply, and the response was not a safety finding.

For NAD (preservesExistingArticle) it calls patchPreserved(), which persists strtr(phraseReplacements) into overview/conclusion/background/description/peptide_full_name and faq answers. The stored NAD text may therefore already equal the rendered text. The strtr guard accepts both states, because strtr of already-replaced text is a no-op. new_value contains no replacement source phrase, so a later framing-seeder run leaves it unchanged.
